claims.evidence: NIDDK: hollow, muscular organ that fills with urine. OpenStax: bladder collects urine from both ureters. StatPearls: lesser pelvis.
claims.newSentence: The urinary bladder is a hollow, muscular organ in the pelvis that collects urine from the ureters.

claims.evidence: NIDDK: brain signals sphincters to relax, then signals the muscular bladder wall to tighten, squeezing urine through the urethra.
claims.newSentence: To empty it, the brain signals the sphincters to relax and then signals the muscular bladder wall to tighten, squeezing urine through the urethra.

claims.evidence: NIDDK: sphincter muscles remain contracted to keep urine in the bladder while it fills; they stay closed until the brain signals.
claims.newSentence: While the bladder fills, the sphincter muscles stay contracted to keep urine in.

claims.evidence: OpenStax 25.2: urethra starts at the trigone area at the bladder base and carries urine from the bladder to outside the body.
StatPearls Bladder: lesser pelvis when empty, extends into abdominal cavity when full, just posterior to pubic symphysis; higher in children.
claims.newSentence: Lesser pelvis just behind the pubic symphysis in adults; extends into the abdominal cavity when full

claims.evidence: StatPearls Histology: urothelium, lamina propria, muscularis propria (detrusor), serosa or adventitia. OpenStax glossary: detrusor is smooth muscle.
Triangle with corners at ureteric and urethral openings confirmed (StatPearls Cystoscopy). 'Smooth' and 'richest in receptors' only in patents; StatPearls says most stretch-sensitive.
claims.newSentence: Triangular area of the bladder floor with corners at the two ureteric openings and the urethral opening; the most sensitive region for stretch receptors

claims.evidence: StatPearls Sphincter Urethrae: internal sphincter is involuntary smooth muscle; external sphincter is striated skeletal muscle under voluntary control.
StatPearls Internal Iliac Arteries: inferior vesical is an anterior-division branch. StatPearls Bladder: superior vesical is a hypogastric (internal iliac) branch; both supply the bladder.
StatPearls Bladder: the lymphatics of the bladder mostly drain into the external iliac lymph nodes.
NHS: a long, thin tube with a small camera is put into the urethra and moved through into the bladder.
StatPearls Bladder: lesser pelvis when empty, extends into the abdominal cavity when full; situated just posterior to the pubic symphysis.
claims.newSentence: In adults the bladder lies in the lesser pelvis when it is empty, just behind the pubic symphysis, and extends into the abdominal cavity when it is full.

claims.evidence: StatPearls Bladder: apex (or dome), body, fundus and neck. 'Or base' for the fundus was not retrieved, so dropped.
claims.newSentence: It is described as having four parts: the apex or dome, the body, the fundus, and the neck.

claims.evidence: StatPearls: superior and part of posterior bladder surfaces are covered by peritoneum; exact StatPearls page not certain (see notes).
claims.newSentence: Peritoneum covers the superior surface and part of the posterior surface of the bladder.

claims.evidence: StatPearls: rectum posterior to the bladder in males. OpenStax: prostate immediately inferior to bladder. 'Base firmly attached to prostate' not found.
claims.newSentence: Where a prostate is present, the rectum lies behind the bladder and the prostate lies immediately below it.

claims.evidence: StatPearls: in females the anterior vaginal wall lies behind the bladder. 'Base and urethra rest on it' not found; PMC pages returned no body text.
claims.newSentence: Where a vagina is present, its anterior wall lies behind the bladder.

claims.evidence: StatPearls Bladder: inferiorly, the muscles of the pelvic diaphragm support the bladder.
claims.newSentence: The muscles of the pelvic diaphragm support the bladder from below.

claims.evidence: No StatPearls text found on caesarean-section bladder injury or surgeons identifying the bladder; directive wording and off-topic for anatomy.
Layers confirmed, but sources vary on the layer count and 'connective tissue with vessels and nerve endings' was not retrieved; rewritten without a count.
claims.newSentence: The bladder wall is made up of an inner urothelial lining, the lamina propria beneath it, the detrusor muscle (the muscularis propria) and an outer serosa or adventitia.

claims.evidence: StatPearls Histology: urothelium has more layers when relaxed and reorganises into fewer layers in the distended bladder without structural damage.
claims.newSentence: The urothelium has more layers when the bladder is relaxed and reorganises into fewer layers as the bladder fills, without structural damage.

claims.evidence: OpenStax 25.2: highly stretchable organ of crisscrossing smooth-muscle bands. 'Spiral, longitudinal, circular bundles' appeared only in a patent; removed.
claims.newSentence: The detrusor is made of crisscrossing bands of smooth muscle, and the whole organ is highly stretchable.

claims.evidence: StatPearls Cystoscopy: trigone is a triangular part of the bladder floor with corners at the internal urethral opening and two ureteral openings.
claims.newSentence: On the inner surface the trigone is a triangular area of the bladder floor whose corners are the two ureteric openings and the opening of the urethra.

claims.evidence: 'Highest concentration of receptors' came only from patents. StatPearls Bladder: the trigone is the most sensitive region for stretch receptors; used instead.
claims.newSentence: It is the most sensitive region of the bladder for stretch receptors.

claims.evidence: The anchoring and no-rugae wording was found only in implant patents, not in OpenStax or any cited publisher page.
OpenStax 25.2: the urethra starts at the trigone area at the bladder base, between the ureteral openings.
OpenStax: male urethra passes through prostate just below bladder and carries urine and semen. The four-region split with preprostatic was not retrieved; removed.
claims.newSentence: The male urethra passes through the prostate gland just below the bladder and also carries semen.

claims.evidence: StatPearls: two urethral sphincters that differ in tissue type and control. 'Contracting narrows the urethra to slow or stop urination' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: There are two urethral sphincters, an internal one and an external one, which differ in tissue type and control.

claims.evidence: StatPearls: internal sphincter is involuntary smooth muscle at the bladder neck, continuous with the detrusor; helps prevent semen flowing back into the bladder.
claims.newSentence: The internal sphincter is smooth muscle at the bladder neck, continuous with the detrusor, and works involuntarily; in the male urethra it also helps stop semen flowing back into the bladder during ejaculation.

claims.evidence: StatPearls: external sphincter is skeletal, voluntary, with somatic innervation from the pudendal nerve. OpenStax: skeletal muscle, relaxed consciously to void.
StatPearls Sphincter Urethrae: urinary incontinence is commonly tied to urethral sphincter pathology.
claims.newSentence: Urinary incontinence is commonly linked to problems with the urethral sphincters.

claims.evidence: StatPearls Bladder: superior and inferior vesical arteries supply the bladder; superior (from hypogastric artery) supplies the upper part; vaginal artery replaces inferior vesical.
claims.newSentence: The superior and inferior vesical arteries provide the blood supply to the bladder, with the superior vesical artery, a branch of the internal iliac artery, supplying the upper part. Where a vagina is present, the vaginal artery replaces the inferior vesical artery.

claims.evidence: StatPearls Bladder: blood drains via the vesical venous plexus into the internal iliac vein; lymphatics mostly drain into external iliac nodes.
claims.newSentence: Venous blood drains through the vesical venous plexus into the internal iliac vein, and lymph drains mostly to the external iliac nodes.

claims.evidence: StatPearls: parasympathetic, sympathetic and somatic fibres; parasympathetic from sacral nerves via pelvic splanchnic nerves. 'Pelvic plexus' not named in results.
claims.newSentence: The bladder receives parasympathetic, sympathetic and somatic nerve fibres, and the parasympathetic fibres arise from the sacral spinal nerves and form the pelvic splanchnic nerves.

claims.evidence: OpenStax 25.2: parasympathetic activity contracts detrusor and relaxes internal sphincter; sympathetic input via hypogastric nerves suppresses detrusor contraction. StatPearls agrees.
StatPearls: sensory information from the superior bladder wall follows the sympathetic pathway; from the inferior part it follows parasympathetic nerves.
claims.newSentence: Sensory information from the upper bladder wall follows the sympathetic pathway, whereas that from the lower part follows the parasympathetic nerves.

claims.evidence: StatPearls describes a hollow muscular organ acting as a reservoir for urine; 'excretory organ' was not retrieved, so dropped.
claims.newSentence: The bladder acts as a reservoir for urine.

claims.evidence: StatPearls Physiology, Urination: storage is maintained by the pontine storage centre; voiding then begins; spinobulbospinal reflex switches between them.
NIDDK: muscles of the bladder wall remain relaxed while the bladder fills, and sphincter muscles remain contracted to keep urine in.
claims.newSentence: During storage the detrusor, the muscle of the bladder wall, stays relaxed as the bladder fills, while the sphincter muscles stay contracted to keep urine in.

claims.evidence: StatPearls: pontine storage centre maintains spinal sympathetic tone to bladder and somatic stimulation of urethral sphincter; hypogastric nerves relax detrusor; pudendal supplies external sphincter.
claims.newSentence: Sympathetic tone to the bladder, carried by the hypogastric nerves, keeps the detrusor relaxed, and somatic stimulation through the pudendal nerve keeps the external sphincter closed.

claims.evidence: StatPearls: voiding begins with increased afferent input from detrusor; higher centres start voiding. NCBI-hosted pages: Barrington's nucleus is the pontine micturition centre, voiding-reflex hub.
claims.newSentence: Voiding begins with increased sensory input from the detrusor, and higher brain centres start voluntary voiding. In the brainstem, the pontine micturition centre, also known as Barrington's nucleus, is the hub of the voiding reflex.

claims.evidence: StatPearls: the detrusor contracts and the urethral sphincter opens, allowing urinary flow. NIDDK: sphincters relax, bladder wall tightens, squeezing urine through the urethra.
NHS cystitis page: cystitis is a bladder infection.
claims.newSentence: Cystitis is a bladder infection.

claims.evidence: NHS: it often gets better by itself, but may sometimes be treated with antibiotics.
NHS: pain, burning or stinging when you pee; needing to pee more often and urgently; dark, cloudy or strong-smelling pee; pain low in tummy.
OpenStax 25.2: the shorter female urethra contributes to the higher incidence of bladder infections in females.
claims.newSentence: The shorter female urethra contributes to the higher incidence of bladder infections in females.

claims.evidence: NHS cystitis page: pain in the back (just under the ribs), high temperature or feeling sick can mean a kidney infection needing prompt treatment.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says pain in the back, a high temperature or feeling sick can point to a kidney infection, which needs prompt treatment.

claims.evidence: NHS cystitis page: see a GP if your child has symptoms or you are a man. 'Always assessed' not retrieved; neutral wording kept.
claims.newSentence: The NHS advises seeing a GP for cystitis symptoms in children and in people with a prostate.

claims.evidence: NIDDK: chronic, long-lasting bladder pain; tends to intensify as urine accumulates and ease once emptied; severity from mild pelvic pressure or tenderness to intense pain.
claims.newSentence: Interstitial cystitis, also called bladder pain syndrome, is a chronic, or long-lasting, condition in which there is pain in the bladder. The pain tends to intensify as urine accumulates and to ease once the bladder is emptied, and severity varies from mild pelvic pressure or tenderness to intense bladder pain.

claims.evidence: NHS urinary incontinence page describes stress, urge, mixed and overflow incontinence.
NHS: stress incontinence is urine leaking when the bladder is under pressure, e.g. coughing or laughing. 'Sudden extra pressure', sneezing, heavy lifting not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: In stress incontinence urine leaks out at times when the bladder is under pressure, for example when coughing or laughing.

claims.evidence: NHS: urge incontinence is a sudden, very intense need to pass urine, unable to delay; usually linked to detrusor overactivity, known as overactive bladder.
claims.newSentence: Urge incontinence is a sudden and very intense need to pass urine that cannot be delayed, and it is usually linked to overactivity of the detrusor muscle, known as an overactive bladder.

claims.evidence: NCI: almost all bladder cancers are urothelial carcinomas; these cells line the bladder and other urinary organs.
claims.newSentence: Almost all bladder cancers are urothelial carcinomas, which start in the urothelial cells that line the bladder and other urinary organs.

claims.evidence: NCI: most common symptom; bleeding can be intermittent, sometimes only trace amounts found by a test. NHS: bright pink, red or dark brown.
claims.newSentence: Blood in the urine is the most common symptom of bladder cancer; it may look pink, red or dark brown, may come and go, or may be found only on a laboratory test.

claims.evidence: NHS: see a GP even with no other symptoms. NCI: infections or kidney or bladder stones could be the cause. No source says 'usually'; removed.
claims.newSentence: It can also have other causes, such as urinary tract infections or kidney or bladder stones, but the NHS advises having blood in the urine checked by a GP even when there are no other symptoms.

claims.evidence: NHS: a test that lets a clinician look inside the bladder; 'lining' was not stated.
claims.newSentence: Cystoscopy lets a clinician look inside the bladder.

claims.evidence: NHS: a long, thin tube with a small camera is gently put into the urethra and moved through into the bladder.
NHS (flexible cystoscopy): local anaesthetic gel numbs the urethra; saline inflates the bladder for a clearer view. Rigid version uses general or spinal anaesthetic.
claims.newSentence: In a flexible cystoscopy, local anaesthetic gel numbs the urethra and saline is run into the bladder to inflate it, which makes it easier to see inside.

claims.evidence: StatPearls Cystoscopy: examiner inspects the floor and trigone and records the number and position of the ureteral orifices.
claims.newSentence: At cystoscopy the examiner inspects the bladder floor and trigone and records the number and position of the ureteric openings.

claims.evidence: NCI diagnosis page: doctor may order urine lab tests first; when bladder cancer is suspected, the most useful diagnostic test is cystoscopy.
claims.newSentence: For suspected bladder cancer the NCI says a doctor may order urine tests first and that cystoscopy is the most useful diagnostic test.

notes: 1) Word counts use the validator's method (intro plus section bodies); with key facts included: before 1101, after 1133. 2) Classification describes each sentence as originally written: 'supported' = every assertion confirmed (wording may be adjusted); 'unsupported' = at least one assertion not confirmed, with the confirmed remainder kept as an edited sentence, or the sentence removed (c18, c24). No sentence was classed textbook, wrong or unsafe, and every claim had at least one search. 3) Please spot-check these, because search summaries do not always name the exact page behind a quotation: c14 (peritoneal covering: the summary named only 'a StatPearls entry'; the Bladder chapter was the first link returned), c40 (Barrington's nucleus as the pontine micturition centre came from NCBI-hosted pages, possibly not the cited Physiology, Urination page), c33 and c35 (nerve statements, taken to be from the Bladder chapter). 4) OpenStax 25.2 could not be read in full and the domain filter let USPTO patent pages through. The wording behind c23 ('highest concentration of sensory nerve receptors'), c24 (anchored, no rugae) and the spiral, longitudinal and circular bundles in c21 matched patent text, so those were removed or replaced with StatPearls wording. 5) Sources disagree on the bladder layer count, so no count is given (c19). One review treats the vaginal artery as the same vessel as the inferior vesical artery; the article follows StatPearls (the vaginal artery replaces it). 6) A 2023 eLife paper (PMC10942786) argues that pelvic organs receive no parasympathetic innervation; the article keeps the textbook model stated by OpenStax and StatPearls. 7) c47: the NHS says 'man'; the draft's neutral wording 'people with a prostate' was kept, please confirm it is acceptable. The NHS urgency level for children and males differs between its cystitis and UTI pages, so the article says only 'seeing a GP'. 8) c57 now specifies a flexible cystoscopy because the NHS says the rigid version usually needs a general or spinal anaesthetic. 9) c31 gained one retrieved nuance (the vaginal artery replaces the inferior vesical artery) so the inferior vesical artery is not generalised; that the inferior vesical artery is an internal iliac branch comes from StatPearls Internal Iliac Arteries (c09). 10) References: dropped NCI PDQ screening, PMC4566164 and PMC1472875 (no body text returned; nothing relies on them); added StatPearls Cystoscopy and Internal Iliac Arteries; stripped '?redirect=true' from the NCI bladder URL; this article has no PubMed stone-location URL. StatPearls URLs keep the 'sites/books' form the search returned. 11) No numbers beyond descriptive anatomy were added (spinal levels, lengths and capacities omitted).
